Core explanation · 00:00–04:59

I'm Professor Ananda, Department of Electronics and Communication Engineering.

Key details

  • Today, we're going to see the parallel clipper, but the last class we have seen the series clipper.
  • The series clipper are those which is used to clip off the waveform that is not required and without disturbing the other part of the waveform.
  • The analysis of the parallel configuration is very similar to that of the series configuration.
  • The other end of the resistor is connected to the diode.
  • When the diode is on, we represent it by a short circuit.
  • When the diode is off, represented as an open circuit.
  • When it's represented as an open circuit, the voltage across the diode is same as the input applied.
  • The same thing applies to any input in the place of a square if you use the triangle as shown.
  • Determine the Vout for the network of the figure 16.
  • DC voltage, V is equal to 4 volts, with the positive side connected to the positive side of the diode and negative side connected to the ground.
  • And the diode positive side is connected to the resistor, where the voltage applied.
  • VI is applied to the one end of the resistor, other end is connected to the supply voltage.
  • DC voltage, and we see that the negative is in series with the positive.
  • That means the applied voltage here will get minus with the V.
  • That means to say...
  • So we'll try to understand that with the next step.
  • Then, in other words, when the diode is on, the output will be 4 volts.
  • This we need to prove now.
  • Then when the diode is in open circuit, that is the off state, the current through the series network will be 0, and the voltage drop across the resistor will be 0.
  • That will be Vout is equal to VI.
  • During the positive half cycle, transition from 0 to T/2, diode is on.
  • How do we represent?
  • 4 volts there.
  • And the diode is 0, and transition 0 instead of transition.
  • That is why VI greater than 4 volts, Vout=VI.
  • That means to say, if VI is greater than 4 volts, then VA greater than 4 volts, diode is off.
  • How do you represent that?

Example or application from the lecture

  • Let us have a refresh of that.
  • Now let us go ahead with the parallel clipper, first without bias, then with bias.
  • So let us go with the clipper with a bias, with an example.

Core explanation · 05:00–09:59

Greater than 4, less than 4, 4 volts, greater than 4.

Key details

  • VK is equal to 0.7.
  • During the transition voltage, using the ID is equal to 0 or VD is equal to 0.7 volts and draw current in the network as shown in the figure 19.
  • In the previous case, it was 0, VD was 0.
  • The total voltage applied is, we'll add or subtract, so 3.3.
  • It's subtract here because I have minus plus or plus minus.
  • It's 3.3.
  • In the previous case, it was 4 volts there.
  • Whereas now, the total voltage, sum of the voltage here is 4 minus 0.7 is 3.3 we get.
  • Then during the negative half cycle what we notice is, same as an input.
  • The input voltage is 16 here, and hence we follow up to 16 the same waveform, and T/2 to T, the same 3.3 will be continued.
  • The summary of the series clipper and the parallel clipper.
  • In a positive clipper, the positive part is missing here.
  • The circuit is this.
  • Hence we call it as a negative clipper.
  • Then, coming to the bias.
  • The positive was missing in the previous case.
  • Now positive is there, but it got clipped off because of the voltage available here.
  • Presence of the voltage over here.
  • This is because of the transition happened because of the clipper.
  • Because of the voltage applied there.
  • Then come to the simple parallel clipper with ideal diodes.
  • The positive part is missing, positive clipper.
  • Negative part is missing, negative clipper.
